lessons.title: SELECT basics
lessons.explain: SELECT picks columns; FROM names the table; WHERE filters rows; ORDER BY sorts. This is the backbone of every query.
objectives: Retrieve and filter rows using SELECT, FROM, WHERE, and ORDER BY
Explain how SELECT changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect SELECT with WHERE and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Forgetting that SQL clauses have a required order (SELECT...FROM...WHERE...ORDER BY), not the order they're logically explained in.

lessons.title: Joins
lessons.explain: A JOIN combines rows from two tables on a matching key. INNER keeps only matches; LEFT keeps all left rows even without a match.
objectives: Combine rows from two tables using INNER and LEFT JOIN
Explain how INNER JOIN changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect INNER JOIN with LEFT JOIN and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Joining tables with no ON condition, producing a cartesian product instead of matched pairs.

lessons.title: Aggregation
lessons.explain: GROUP BY collapses rows into groups; aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG) summarize each group. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
lessons.example:
SELECT category, COUNT(*)
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
objectives: Summarize groups of rows using GROUP BY and aggregate functions
Explain how GROUP BY changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect GROUP BY with HAVING and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Using WHERE instead of HAVING to filter on an aggregate value -- WHERE runs before aggregation happens.
lessons.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows into groups; aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG) summarize each group. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

lessons.title: Filtering, sorting & limiting results
objectives: Use WHERE, ORDER BY, DISTINCT, and LIMIT together
Explain how WHERE changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect WHERE with ORDER BY and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens. ORDER BY sorts the result -- add DESC for descending order.
examples:
SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers
WHERE country = 'UAE'
ORDER BY city DESC
LIMIT 5;
commonMistakes: Forgetting that WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so it can't reference an aggregate like COUNT(*) -- that needs HAVING instead.
lessons.careerRelevance: Filtering, sorting, and limiting are the most frequently written parts of everyday SQL.
lessons.explain: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens. ORDER BY sorts the result -- add DESC for descending order.

lessons.title: Keys & constraints
objectives: Explain primary keys, foreign keys, NOT NULL, and UNIQUE
Explain how primary key changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect primary key with foreign key and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A primary key is a column (or set of columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a table -- no two rows can share one. A foreign key links a row to a row in another table, enforcing that the reference actually exists.
commonMistakes: Adding a foreign key column without actually enforcing (or checking) that the referenced row exists -- this silently allows orphaned references.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correct keys and constraints are what keep a real database's data consistent and trustworthy.

lessons.title: Working with NULL
objectives: Compare against NULL correctly
Explain how NULL changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect NULL with IS NULL and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: NULL means 'no value,' and it doesn't equal anything -- not even another NULL. Comparing with = or != against NULL never matches, even for rows that ARE NULL; you must use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL instead.
examples:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;      -- correct: finds active users
SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at = NULL;        -- WRONG: matches nothing, ever
commonMistakes: Writing `column = NULL` or `column != NULL` -- these silently match zero rows, which is a very easy mistake to miss.
lessons.careerRelevance: NULL-handling bugs are one of the most common real-world SQL mistakes, worth internalizing early.
lessons.explain: NULL means 'no value,' and it doesn't equal anything -- not even another NULL. Comparing with = or != against NULL never matches, even for rows that ARE NULL; you must use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL instead.

lessons.title: Types of joins & join pitfalls
objectives: Distinguish INNER and LEFT JOIN, and avoid accidental cartesian products
Explain how INNER JOIN changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect INNER JOIN with LEFT JOIN and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, with NULLs filling in for any unmatched right-table columns.
commonMistakes: Writing FROM a, b with no WHERE/ON condition linking them -- this produces a cartesian product, not the intended matched pairs.
lessons.careerRelevance: Choosing the right join type correctly is one of the most common real interview and code-review topics in SQL.
lessons.explain: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, with NULLs filling in for any unmatched right-table columns.

lessons.title: GROUP BY & HAVING in depth
objectives: Aggregate data with GROUP BY and filter groups with HAVING
Explain how GROUP BY changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect GROUP BY with HAVING and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows sharing the same value in a column into groups, letting you compute one aggregate (COUNT, SUM, AVG) per group. HAVING filters those GROUPS after aggregation -- it's evaluated later than WHERE, which is why HAVING can reference an aggregate like COUNT(*) but WHERE can't.
examples:
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS num_items, AVG(price) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
commonMistakes: Using HAVING for a condition that doesn't need aggregation (it belongs in WHERE, which runs earlier and is usually more efficient).
lessons.careerRelevance: GROUP BY + HAVING is the core toolkit for any real reporting or analytics query.
lessons.explain: GROUP BY collapses rows sharing the same value in a column into groups, letting you compute one aggregate (COUNT, SUM, AVG) per group. lessons.example:
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS num_items, AVG(price) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

lessons.title: Modifying data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
objectives: Add, change, and remove rows safely
Explain how INSERT changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect INSERT with UPDATE and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: INSERT adds new rows. UPDATE changes existing rows (always pair it with a WHERE clause, or every row gets updated).
commonMistakes: Running UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause -- this affects every single row in the table, usually not what was intended.
lessons.careerRelevance: These are the most consequential SQL statements to get right, since mistakes here directly change real data.
lessons.explain: INSERT adds new rows. UPDATE changes existing rows (always pair it with a WHERE clause, or every row gets updated).

lessons.title: Indexes & performance basics
objectives: Explain what an index does and its trade-offs
Explain how index changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect index with CREATE INDEX and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An index is a data structure that speeds up lookups on a column, similar to a book's index -- the database can jump directly to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table. The trade-off: indexes use extra storage and slightly slow down writes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), since the index has to be updated too.
examples:
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
-- now WHERE email = '...' can use the index instead of scanning every row
commonMistakes: Adding an index to every column 'just in case' -- each index adds real write overhead, so they should target columns actually used often in WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding indexes is essential once queries need to run fast against real, large tables.
lessons.explain: An index is a data structure that speeds up lookups on a column, similar to a book's index -- the database can jump directly to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table. lessons.title: Pattern matching & subqueries
objectives: Use LIKE for pattern matching and write a basic subquery
Explain how LIKE changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect LIKE with subquery and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: LIKE '%text%' matches any value containing 'text' anywhere -- % is a wildcard for any sequence of characters. A subquery is a query nested inside another, often used in a WHERE clause to filter against a dynamically computed set of values.
commonMistakes: Assuming LIKE 'smith%' and LIKE '%smith%' behave the same -- the % placement changes whether it matches the start, end, or anywhere in the text.
lessons.careerRelevance: Pattern matching and subqueries come up constantly in real reporting and search-style queries.
lessons.explain: LIKE '%text%' matches any value containing 'text' anywhere -- % is a wildcard for any sequence of characters. A subquery is a query nested inside another, often used in a WHERE clause to filter against a dynamically computed set of values.

lessons.title: Window Functions & CTEs
objectives: Use CTEs to structure complex queries and window functions to compute running totals and rankings without collapsing rows
Explain how CTE changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect CTE with common table expression and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A CTE (Common Table Expression, written with WITH) names a subquery so you can reference it like a temporary table, making a complex multi-step query readable instead of deeply nested.
examples:
WITH monthly_totals AS (
  SELECT customer_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id, month
)
SELECT customer_id, month, total,
  SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY month) AS running_total
FROM monthly_totals;
-- running_total accumulates per customer, resetting for each new customer,
-- while every row (one per customer per month) stays visible -- unlike GROUP BY,
-- which would have collapsed this into one row per customer
commonMistakes: Reaching for GROUP BY when what's actually needed is a running total or per-row ranking -- GROUP BY collapses rows into one per group, which loses the per-row detail a window function (SUM().
lessons.careerRelevance: Window functions and CTEs are the dividing line between basic SQL and the SQL fluency real data-facing interviews and dashboards actually require -- a very common interview and take-home assessment topic.
lessons.explain: A CTE (Common Table Expression, written with WITH) names a subquery so you can reference it like a temporary table, making a complex multi-step query readable instead of deeply nested.
lessons.example:

FROM monthly_totals;

-- while every row (one per customer per month) stays visible -- unlike GROUP BY,
-- which would have collapsed this into one row per customer

exercises.hint: joining orders to order_items multiplies each order's row once per item it contains, so summing order_amount after the join adds that same order total in multiple times -- fix by aggregating order_items separately first (or summing order-level amounts BEFORE the join, e.g. with a CTE), not after a row-multiplying join

description: Query and shape data — SELECT through window functions.

interviewPreparation.q: Why might joining two tables and then summing a column give a wildly inflated result?
interviewPreparation.a: If the join has a one-to-many relationship (like orders to order_items), each row on the 'one' side gets duplicated once per matching row on the 'many' side -- summing a column from the 'one' side after that join adds the same value in multiple times. Aggregate the many-side table first (often with a CTE), or aggregate before joining, to avoid this.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between GROUP BY and a window function, and when would you need a window function specifically?
interviewPreparation.a: GROUP BY collapses rows into one output row per group, losing per-row detail. A window function (SUM()/RANK()/ROW_NUMBER() OVER ...) computes an aggregate or ranking across related rows WITHOUT collapsing them -- needed whenever you want the aggregate value AND the individual row detail together, like a running total shown alongside every original row.

interviewPreparation.q: Why use a CTE instead of a deeply nested subquery?
interviewPreparation.a: Readability and maintainability, mainly -- a CTE names each step of a multi-stage calculation so the query reads top-to-bottom like a sequence of steps, instead of nesting subqueries inside subqueries that are hard to trace. They're not usually faster, just clearer to write, read, and debug.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you check whether a slow query is actually using an index?
interviewPreparation.a: Run EXPLAIN (or the database's equivalent query-plan tool) and check whether it shows an index scan or a full table/sequential scan on the relevant table -- a full scan on a large table for a query that should be selective usually means the index either doesn't exist or doesn't match what the query actually filters or joins on.

interviewPreparation.q: Why does `WHERE column = NULL` never match any rows, even when the column genuinely contains NULLs?
interviewPreparation.a: NULL represents an unknown value, and SQL's three-valued logic means comparing anything to NULL with `=` returns unknown, not true -- even NULL = NULL is unknown, not true. Use `IS NULL` (or `IS NOT NULL`) specifically, which is designed to test for NULL correctly.

careerApplications: Directly asked about in most SWE and data interviews; used daily on the job.

capstone.title: Answer real business questions with advanced, correct SQL
capstone.description: Given a realistic multi-table schema (orders, customers, products, order items), write a set of queries that would genuinely power a business dashboard: correct joins that don't silently inflate results, meaningful aggregation, and at least one query using a CTE and a window function together (e.g. month-over-month running revenue per customer, or top-N-per-category using RANK()). This capstone is about SQL correctness and real analytical thinking, not just syntax -- a query that runs without error but returns the wrong number is worse than one that fails loudly.
deliverables: A set of queries answering realistic business questions (e.g. top customers, monthly revenue trend, best-selling products per category)
At least one query using a CTE to structure a multi-step calculation readably
At least one query using a window function (running total, ranking, or moving average) that would be wrong or impossible to express cleanly with GROUP BY alone
A written note on one query you initially got wrong (a join that inflated results, a NULL that silently excluded rows) and how you caught and fixed it
EXPLAIN output (or equivalent) for at least one query, with a note on whether it's using an index or doing a full scan
capstone.portfolioTips: The written note about a query you got wrong and caught is genuinely more convincing than a folder of queries that 'just work' -- it's concrete evidence you can verify your own SQL rather than trusting that it compiled.

industryUsage.usage: Relies heavily on SQL analysts and engineers writing correct, non-trivial queries (window functions, CTEs) directly against large production-scale datasets to answer real business questions.

SQL proficiency, including window functions and correct join handling, is a commonly tested skill in both data-focused and general software engineering interviews, given how much internal tooling is built on top of SQL analytics.

Given its data-heavy product surface, correct and performant SQL -- including avoiding join-based row inflation and knowing when to index -- is a practical, everyday engineering skill, not just an interview topic.
